newsitem.title: FRANCE: European parliament president clashes with France.
newsitem.headline: European parliament president clashes with France.

text.p: The European Parliament president called off talks with France's foreign minister on Wednesday in protest at his branding the legislature "not worthy of the name" after it urged Paris to withdraw a disputed immigration bill.
Jose-Maria Gil-Robles, on an inaugural visit to France, called Herve de Charette's remarks on television "an unacceptable judgement on the European Parliament, its role and its dignity".
But the Spanish conservative later played down the incident, saying he had no intention of drawing out their differences.
"Mr de Charette said what he thought he had to say, and I took the stance dictated by his remarks," he told reporters. "Certainly I see no point in prolonging this."
Gil-Robles initially had demanded a clarification of de Charette's criticisms, saying they may have gone "beyond his thoughts".

But an unrepentant de Charette promptly renewed his assault, telling the National Assembly the European Parliament had overstepped its powers by calling on the French government to withdraw the bill that would clamp down further on illegal immigration and widen police powers.
"It is particularly shocking to see the European Parliament meddling in the national legislative process," he said.

He blamed France's opposition Socialists for proposing the motion adopted in Strasbourg by 106-101 votes last Thursday. The motion, inserted in a resolution "on racism, xenophobia and the extreme right", was proposed by leftist French members.

De Charette sparked Gil-Robles' protests by saying in an early morning television interview: "Once again, I have to say with regret...that the European Parliament shows that it is not yet a parliament worthy of the name."

Officials said the coordinated French attack, launched by President Jacques Chirac and joined by National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and Senate President Rene Monory, suggested Paris would oppose any increase in the Strasbourg-based legislature's powers in the current reform of European Union institutions.
Germany, France's closest EU partner, traditionally advocates extending the parliament's role.

"Naturally, we have, and I am sure you have, the greatest respect for the European Parliament," de Charette said to jeers from his centre-right coalition in the National Assembly minutes before his scrapped appointment with Gil-Robles.
"But if it wants to play an important role in future, it will have to respect national sovereignty," he added. "We intend that this protest (by Chirac) will have consequences."

The verbal clash also gave France's Gaullist rulers an opportunity to rally mainstream conservative and hard right voters behind a nationalist banner in the face of an assembly which the French have traditionally disdained.
The immigration bill, which would close loopholes in France's already tough immigration laws, is the subject of a stormy debate in the French parliament.
It triggered clashes in Paris between police and protesters on Tuesday in which 40 police were hurt.

Chirac, who slammed "unacceptable interference" in France's internal affairs when he met Gil-Robles on Tuesday, nurses bitter memories of a hostile reception over French nuclear testing when he addressed the parliament in July 1995.
Leftist and ecologist parliamentarians heckled and jeered him in the Strasbourg chamber, chanting "No No No" and waving banners bearing a mushroom cloud and the word "Non" in French.
The opposition Socialists accused Chirac on Wednesday of diversionary tactics.
"This instance shows again the hostility of part of the French coalition to the European Parliament. It's a premeditated offensive," Socialist Euro-deputy Elisabeth Guigou said.
